lessons.title: Reconciliation, keys and the Fiber architecture
lessons.summary: What the virtual DOM really buys you, how reconciliation and keys decide identity and state, and how Fiber, lanes and the commit phases make rendering interruptible.
lessons.body:
## The core idea React lets you describe the UI for the current state, and it works out which DOM operations get the page from what it shows now to what you described. Working that out is **reconciliation**. **Fiber** is the engine that has done it since React 16 (2017). Fiber splits rendering into small units of work, so React can pause, prioritise and throw away work. That ability is what makes transitions, Suspense and streaming possible. Two myths to clear up first: - **"The virtual DOM is faster than the DOM."** It is not. A virtual DOM adds work: building element objects, diffing them, and only then touching the DOM. Hand-written DOM updates are always at least as fast. React's argument is that you write declarative code and React keeps the DOM writes close to minimal for you. Svelte and Solid get similar or better speed with no virtual DOM at all, because they compile updates straight down to DOM operations. - **"React re-renders the DOM on every state change."** Rendering means calling your components and diffing their output. The DOM only changes where the output changed. Dan Abramov's essay "React as a UI Runtime" (overreacted.io) is the best long read on this model. It describes React as a runtime that manages a tree of "host instances" (DOM nodes) for you. ## Step 1: elements are cheap descriptions JSX compiles to plain objects: ```tsx // becomes roughly: const el = { type: Button, key: null, props: { kind: "primary", children: "Save" } }; ``` When your component runs, it returns a tree of these objects. React compares the new tree with the tree it built last time. A perfect diff between two arbitrary trees costs O(n^3), which would be far too slow. The old reconciliation docs describe two heuristics React uses instead, which bring the cost down to O(n): 1. **Different type means a different subtree.** If a `div` becomes a `section`, or `` becomes ``, React unmounts the old subtree, which destroys its state and DOM, and mounts a new one. It does not try to reuse anything. 2. **Keys identify children across renders.** Within a list of siblings, React matches old and new children by `key`. Without keys it matches them by position. When the type at a position stays the same, React keeps the component instance and its state and simply passes in new props. For host elements, it patches only the attributes that changed. ## Step 2: keys are identity, not a warning silencer Keys decide **which state belongs to which item**. ```tsx // Bug: index keys. Delete the first todo and every row's // local state (an open editor, typed text) shifts by one row. {todos.map((t, i) => )} // Correct: a stable id from the data. {todos.map((t) => )} ``` Index keys are fine for a static list that never reorders or filters. Random keys (`key={Math.random()}`) are worse than index keys: every render remounts every row, which throws away state, focus and DOM nodes. Keys also work outside lists. Changing a key is the cleanest way to **reset** a component: ```tsx // A new contact means a fresh form: no effect that copies props into state. ``` The react.dev page "Preserving and Resetting State" puts it this way: state is tied to a **position in the tree**, not to the component function. Same type at the same position (and same key) keeps the state. Anything else resets it. One trap follows from this: if you define a component inside another component, it gets a new type on every render, so it remounts every time. ## Step 3: Fiber, the unit of work Before Fiber, the "stack reconciler" walked the tree recursively and could not stop until it finished. A large update could block the main thread for hundreds of milliseconds, and typing would freeze. Fiber turns the recursion into a loop over a linked data structure that React controls. Each fiber is an object for one component or host node. It holds the type, key, props, state (the hook list), effect flags and pointers: ```text App (fiber) | child v Header ---sibling---> Main ---sibling---> Footer ^ | child | return v List ---> Item ---> Item ``` - `child`, `sibling` and `return` let React walk the tree without the JS call stack, so it can stop after any fiber and resume later. - **Double buffering:** there is a `current` tree (what is on screen) and a `workInProgress` tree being built. Each fiber has an `alternate` pointing at its twin. When the work finishes, React swaps the pointer. A render that gets interrupted or thrown away never touches the screen. ## Step 4: render phase vs commit phase ```text setState / transition / Suspense retry | v schedule an update on a lane | v RENDER PHASE (interruptible in concurrent mode, must be pure) beginWork: call components, reconcile children completeWork: build DOM nodes off-screen, collect effect flags | React may yield to the browser about every 5 ms, | restart if a higher-priority update arrives, | or discard the work entirely v COMMIT PHASE (synchronous, cannot be interrupted) before mutation: read DOM state (e.g. getSnapshotBeforeUpdate) mutation: insert, update and remove DOM nodes; detach old refs layout: attach refs, run useLayoutEffect, before paint | v browser paints | v passive effects: useEffect cleanups, then setups ``` What follows from this: - **The render phase must be pure.** React may call your component several times for one commit, or never commit at all. Side effects in render (subscriptions, mutating module state, analytics calls) will fire twice or leak. StrictMode double-invokes renders in development to surface exactly this. - **The commit phase is all-or-nothing**, so the user never sees a half-updated tree. - `useLayoutEffect` runs before paint, so use it to measure the DOM and fix layout without a flicker. `useEffect` normally runs after paint. Since React 18, effects caused by a discrete input such as a click are flushed before the next discrete event. ## Step 5: lanes and the scheduler Every update gets a **lane**, a bit in a 31-bit mask. Lanes represent priority and also let React batch updates of the same kind together: | Lane (simplified) | Typical source | | --- | --- | | SyncLane | discrete input: click, keydown, `flushSync` | | InputContinuousLane | continuous input: pointermove, scroll | | DefaultLane | updates outside React events (timers, fetch callbacks) | | TransitionLanes | `startTransition`, `useDeferredValue` background renders | | IdleLane / Offscreen | prerendering hidden content (``) | Because lanes are bitmasks, React can cheaply ask "which pending lanes should I work on now?" and render several lanes in one pass. When a click arrives in the middle of a transition render, React leaves the transition work, renders the urgent lane, commits it, and then restarts the transition from the new state. The scheduler yields to the main thread roughly every 5 ms so that input and paint stay responsive. All of this machinery only matters for **concurrent** features. A plain `setState` in a click handler takes the synchronous lane and renders without yielding. Automatic batching (React 18+) groups updates made in the same tick, in timeouts and in promises too, into one render. ## Code: watching it happen ```tsx import { useState, useTransition, Profiler } from "react"; function SlowList({ query }: { query: string }) { const items = []; for (let i = 0; i < 5000; i++) items.push(
  • {query} {i}
    • ); return
      {items}
    ; } export function Search() { const [text, setText] = useState(""); const [query, setQuery] = useState(""); const [isPending, startTransition] = useTransition(); return ( console.log(id, phase, actualMs.toFixed(1))}> { setText(e.target.value); // SyncLane: input stays responsive startTransition(() => setQuery(e.target.value)); // TransitionLane: interruptible }} /> {isPending && Updating...} ); } ``` Type quickly and the input keeps up. React abandons stale `SlowList` renders whenever a new keystroke arrives. Remove the transition and every keystroke blocks for the whole list render. ## Trade-offs and when not to care - The virtual DOM costs memory and CPU on every update. For very high-frequency visual updates (canvas, 60 fps charts, drag positions) you often bypass React state and write to a ref or the DOM directly. - Concurrent rendering makes rendering cheaper to interrupt, but it does not make it cheaper. A 200 ms render in a transition is still 200 ms of CPU, just without blocking input. Fix the slow component first. - Interruptible rendering needs pure components and tear-free stores. External stores must go through `useSyncExternalStore`, otherwise two parts of the tree can read different values within one render ("tearing"). ## Common mistakes and debugging - **Defining components inside components:** the type changes every render, so the subtree remounts, inputs lose focus and effects re-run. - **Index or random keys** on lists that reorder or filter. - **Conditionally switching wrapper types** (`isMobile ?
    :
    ` around a form) and then wondering where the form state went. - **Side effects during render,** which StrictMode exposes as double logs. - **Debugging tools:** turn on React DevTools "Highlight updates when components render", and use the Profiler's "Why did this render?" (record why each component rendered). Chrome Performance traces show long "Render" tasks and the commit. ## In the interview **What they probe:** whether you know that "virtual DOM is fast" is a myth, that rendering is not committing, why keys matter, and whether you can explain Fiber's interruptibility without hand-waving. **60-second answer outline:** 1. React renders components to element trees and reconciles them with the previous tree. Two heuristics keep it O(n): a different type remounts the subtree, and keys match siblings. 2. State lives at a position in the tree, so keys and types decide whether state survives. 3. Fiber represents each component as a linked work unit with current and work-in-progress trees, so the render phase can pause, resume or be discarded. 4. Updates carry lanes (bitmask priorities). Urgent lanes interrupt transitions. 5. The commit phase is synchronous: DOM mutations, then layout effects, then paint, then passive effects. **Follow-ups to expect:** Why must render be pure? What is tearing and how does `useSyncExternalStore` prevent it? Why does an input lose focus when its parent re-renders? (A component defined inline, or a key that changes.) How do Svelte or Solid avoid a virtual DOM?
keyPoints: The virtual DOM is not faster than the DOM; it is a declarative model whose diff keeps DOM writes near-minimal
Reconciliation is O(n): a different type remounts the subtree, and keys match siblings across renders
State belongs to a position in the tree; changing a key or wrapper type resets it
Fiber turns rendering into resumable units of work with current and work-in-progress trees
Updates carry lanes (bitmask priorities); the render phase can be interrupted, the commit phase cannot
interview: Is the virtual DOM actually faster than updating the DOM directly?
What is React Fiber and what problem did it solve?
How does React decide which update to work on first?

check.q: A todo list uses array indexes as keys. The user deletes the first item while the second row has an open inline editor. What happens?
options: React throws a duplicate key error
The editor state stays with the item that is now in the first position, so it appears on the wrong todo
Nothing, React tracks items by content
The whole list unmounts and remounts
check.why: State is matched by key. With index keys, the row at index 1 becomes index 0, so React reuses the wrong instance and its local state.

check.q: Which statement about the render and commit phases in concurrent React is correct?
options: Both phases can be interrupted at any point
Only the commit phase may run more than once per update
useEffect runs during the commit's mutation step, before paint
The render phase may be paused, restarted or discarded; the commit phase runs synchronously to completion
check.why: Interruptibility applies only to the pure render phase. The commit applies DOM mutations and layout effects atomically so users never see a half-updated tree.

check.q: Why does an input lose focus on every keystroke when its component is defined inside the parent component's body?
options: The inner component gets a new function identity each render, so React sees a different type and remounts it
Inline components cannot hold state
React batches the keystrokes and drops focus
StrictMode unmounts components on every render in production
check.why: Type identity drives reconciliation. A component declared inside render is a new type each time, so its subtree, including the focused input, is destroyed and recreated.

lessons.title: React Server Components in depth
lessons.summary: The RSC model: server-only components, the serialised payload, client boundaries, what can cross them, streaming with Suspense, and what the 'use client' and 'use server' directives really mean.
lessons.body:
## The core idea React Server Components (RSC) split one React tree across two environments. **Server Components** run only on the server, either at build time or per request. They can be `async`, read a database or the filesystem directly, and they ship **zero JavaScript** to the browser. **Client Components** are the React you already know: they hydrate in the browser, hold state and handle events. The server renders its part of the tree into a serialised description called the **RSC payload**, sometimes called the Flight format. That payload contains the server-rendered output plus **references** to the client components the browser must load and run. RSC is not SSR. SSR turns a tree into **HTML** so the first paint is fast, and then the whole tree hydrates. RSC turns server components into a **payload React can merge into the live tree**. That works on first load and on every client-side navigation, and it never hydrates the server parts. In a framework like Next.js you get both: the payload is used to SSR HTML for the first request, and only client components hydrate. Dan Abramov's "The Two Reacts" (overreacted.io) is a good framing. UI is a function of both client state and server data, and RSC lets each component run where its inputs live. Josh Comeau's "Making Sense of React Server Components" walks through the same model with diagrams. ## How it works, step by step ```text REQUEST /product/42 | v SERVER: render the Server Component tree ProductPage (server, async) -- awaits db.product(42) ├─ Header (server) ├─ Gallery (CLIENT) -> emitted as a reference: module id + export name + props └─ Suspense └─ Reviews (server, async, slow) -> streams later | v RSC PAYLOAD (streamed rows, simplified) M1: client module ref { id: "gallery.js", name: "Gallery", chunks: [...] } J0: ["div", {}, [

"Blue mug"

, @M1({ images: [...] }), @pending:2 ]] J2: [
    ...reviews...
] <- arrives when the slow query resolves | v CLIENT: React reads the stream, downloads the Gallery chunk, builds the tree, hydrates only Gallery, and fills the Suspense hole when row 2 arrives ``` The row format above is illustrative. The real wire format is an internal detail that changes between versions, so do not depend on it. Key mechanics: 1. **The server tree is resolved to plain data.** Server Components run, their `await`s resolve, and their output is reduced to host elements (`div`, text) plus client references. 2. **Client components are not run on the server for the payload.** React records "render module X with these props here". Their code ships as a normal JS chunk. With SSR they also run on the server once to produce HTML, which is why client components still cannot touch `window` during render. 3. **Streaming:** each `` boundary becomes a hole the server fills later in the same response. The user sees the shell immediately and slow parts arrive as they are ready, in whatever order they finish. 4. **Navigation:** on a client-side route change, the framework fetches a new payload and React reconciles it into the existing tree. Client component state outside the changed segment survives. ## The two directives They are the most misunderstood part of RSC, and they mean completely different things. **`'use client'`** goes at the top of a **module**. It marks the boundary where the server module graph enters the client graph. That file and **everything it imports** becomes client code that gets bundled for the browser. You do not need it on every interactive component, only at the entry points. Components without the directive are not automatically server components either: a file with no directive becomes client code if a client module imports it. **`'use server'`** marks **Server Functions** (called Server Actions when used for mutations). These are async functions the client can call over the network. It does **not** mark Server Components. Server Components need no directive, because in an RSC framework that is the default. The bundler replaces each server function with a reference. Calling it sends a POST with serialised arguments, the function runs on the server, and the result comes back serialised. ```tsx // app/product/[id]/page.tsx (Server Component: no directive) import { db } from "@/lib/db"; import { AddToCart } from "./add-to-cart"; import { addToCart } from "./actions"; export default async function ProductPage({ params }: { params: Promise<{ id: string }> }) { const { id } = await params; const product = await db.product.findUnique({ where: { id } }); // runs on the server only if (!product) return

Not found

; return (

{product.name}

{/* Only serialisable props cross the boundary */}
); } ``` ```tsx // app/product/[id]/add-to-cart.tsx "use client"; import { useTransition } from "react"; export function AddToCart(props: { productId: string; price: number; action: (id: string) => Promise }) { const [pending, start] = useTransition(); return ( ); } ``` ```ts // app/product/[id]/actions.ts "use server"; import { requireUser } from "@/lib/auth"; export async function addToCart(productId: string) { const user = await requireUser(); // every server function is a public endpoint: check auth here // ...validate productId, write the cart row } ``` ## Serialisation: what can cross the boundary Props from a server component to a client component, and arguments and return values of server functions, must be serialisable by React. The react.dev `'use client'` reference lists the supported types: - primitives (string, number, bigint, boolean, undefined, null), and symbols registered with `Symbol.for` - plain objects and arrays made of serialisable values, `Date`, `Map`, `Set`, typed arrays, `ArrayBuffer`, `FormData` - **Promises**, which the client unwraps with `use()`. This lets you start a fetch on the server and stream the result into a client component. - JSX elements, including other server components passed as `children` or slot props - **Server Functions** (functions marked `'use server'`) Not serialisable: ordinary functions (event handlers), class instances (an ORM model, a `Decimal`), closures and DOM nodes. A common fix is to map records to plain DTOs at the boundary. ## The composition pattern: server inside client A client component cannot *import* a server component, because the import would pull it into the client graph. It can still *render* one that is passed in as a prop: ```tsx // Server Component {/* client: holds the active-tab state */} {/* server: queries the DB, rendered on the server */} ``` `BillingSummary` runs on the server. Its output arrives inside the payload as `children`, and `Tabs` places it wherever it likes. This is how you keep interactivity at the leaves and data access at the top. ## Trade-offs and when not to use it **Wins:** less client JS, because heavy libraries such as markdown parsers and syntax highlighters stay on the server. Data fetching sits next to the component without client-side waterfalls. Secrets and DB access stay on the server. Streaming gives a fast first paint. **Costs:** - **A two-world mental model.** Context, state and effects do not exist in server components. Every boundary needs serialisable props. - **Data can be sent twice:** once as HTML and once in the payload that hydrates client components. A 500 KB prop passed to a client component costs 500 KB on the wire twice. Pass IDs or trimmed DTOs. - **Framework coupling.** RSC needs bundler integration. In practice that means Next.js App Router, React Router's RSC support, Waku, or a Parcel or Vite plugin, so it is not a drop-in for an existing SPA. - **Highly interactive apps** (editors, canvases, dashboards with live client state) gain little. Most of the tree is client components anyway. ## Common mistakes and debugging - **`'use client'` on everything** by reflex. You lose the bundle win and push data fetching back to the client. Put it on the leaf that needs state or events. - **Thinking `'use server'` makes a server component.** It creates a public RPC endpoint. - **Leaking secrets through props.** Anything passed to a client component is visible in the payload. Import the `server-only` package in modules that must never reach the client. React's experimental taint APIs (`experimental_taintObjectReference`, `experimental_taintUniqueValue`) can block specific objects or values from being passed. - **Passing a class instance or a callback** gives "Only plain objects can be passed to Client Components" or "Functions cannot be passed directly to Client Components". - **Reading context in a server component.** Wrap providers in a client component and render it high in the tree, passing server content as `children`. - **Debugging:** in Next.js, view the page source to see the inlined payload chunks, and use the Network tab with the `RSC` request header to see navigation payloads. If a component's code shows up in the client bundle unexpectedly, trace which client module imports it. ## In the interview **What they probe:** that you can separate RSC from SSR, explain what the directives really mark, reason about serialisation and payload size, and treat server functions as public endpoints. **60-second answer outline:** 1. Server components run only on the server, can be async and ship no JS. Their output is a serialised payload containing client component references. 2. It is not SSR. SSR makes HTML for the first paint, while RSC makes a mergeable tree for every navigation. Frameworks combine the two. 3. `'use client'` marks the entry into the client module graph. `'use server'` marks callable server functions, not server components. 4. Props crossing the boundary must be serialisable. Pass server components to client components as `children`. 5. Suspense boundaries stream, so slow data does not block the shell. **Follow-ups to expect:** Can a client component render a server component? What happens to client state on navigation? How do you stop a secret leaking into props? Why might RSC increase total bytes on a page?
keyPoints: Server Components run only on the server, can be async and ship no JS; their output is a serialised payload with client references
RSC is not SSR: SSR produces HTML for first paint, RSC produces a mergeable tree for every navigation
'use client' marks the entry into the client module graph; 'use server' marks callable Server Functions, not Server Components
Props crossing the boundary must be serialisable; pass server components to client components as children
Every Server Function is a public endpoint, and every prop is visible in the payload
interview: How are React Server Components different from server-side rendering?
What does the 'use client' directive actually mark, and what does 'use server' mark?
What can you pass as props from a Server Component to a Client Component?

check.q: A file with no directive is imported by a module that starts with 'use client'. Where does its code run?
options: Only on the server, because files without directives are Server Components
Nowhere; the build fails
It becomes part of the client graph and is bundled for the browser
On the edge runtime
check.why: 'use client' marks a boundary in the module graph. Everything imported from a client module is client code, whatever directives it lacks.

check.q: Which prop can NOT be passed from a Server Component to a Client Component?
options: A Promise that resolves to an array of plain objects
An inline arrow function used as an onClick handler
A Date object
A Server Function marked with 'use server'
check.why: Ordinary functions are not serialisable. Promises, Dates and Server Functions are supported by React's serialisation.

check.q: How can a Client Component display a Server Component's output?
options: By receiving it as children or another JSX prop from a server parent
By importing the server component directly
By calling the server component as a function inside useEffect
It is impossible
check.why: Importing would pull the component into the client graph. Passing it as a prop means it renders on the server and arrives in the payload.

lessons.title: Suspense, transitions and concurrent rendering
lessons.summary: How Suspense boundaries work for data and code, how useTransition and useDeferredValue schedule non-urgent work, and what concurrent rendering requires from your code.
lessons.body:
## The core idea Concurrent React has three tools for deciding what the user sees while work is in progress: - **``** declares a loading boundary: "if anything inside is not ready, show this fallback instead." - **`useTransition` / `startTransition`** marks a state update as **non-urgent**. React renders it in the background, can interrupt it, and keeps showing the old UI while it is pending, instead of flashing a fallback. - **`useDeferredValue`** gives you a copy of a value that lags behind during busy periods. Urgent UI uses the fresh value and slow UI uses the deferred one. All three rely on **concurrent rendering**: the render phase can be paused, interrupted and thrown away (see the lesson on reconciliation and Fiber). They do not make code faster. They make React smarter about **what to show and when**. ## How Suspense works A component **suspends** when it cannot finish rendering because something it needs is still loading. In React 19 that happens in three supported ways: 1. Reading a pending promise with `use(promise)`. 2. Rendering a `React.lazy` component whose code has not loaded yet. 3. Using a Suspense-enabled data source. These are frameworks (async Server Components in Next.js, React Router loaders) or libraries such as TanStack Query's `useSuspenseQuery` and Relay. Fetching inside `useEffect` does **not** trigger Suspense. The component already rendered, with empty state, by the time the effect runs. ```text render | +-- use(userPromise) -> promise pending | React stops rendering this subtree and finds the | nearest above it v commit: show that boundary's fallback (siblings outside the boundary still show) | promise resolves -> React retries rendering the subtree v commit: replace the fallback with the content ``` Boundary placement is a design decision. One boundary around the page gives an all-or-nothing reveal. A boundary around every widget gives the "popcorn" effect, with pieces popping in at random. Group content that should appear together, and nest boundaries so the outer shell (nav, heading) shows first and inner details stream in. ```tsx import { Suspense, use } from "react"; function Comments({ commentsPromise }: { commentsPromise: Promise }) { const comments = use(commentsPromise); // suspends until resolved return
    {comments.map((c) =>
  • {c.text}
    • )}
; } export function Post({ post, commentsPromise }: { post: Post; commentsPromise: Promise }) { return (

{post.title}

{post.body}

Loading comments...

}>
); } ``` The promise must be **stable** across renders. If you create it during render (`use(fetch(url))` in a Client Component), every retry creates a new promise and the component suspends forever. Create it in a Server Component, a loader, or a cache, and pass it down. React 19 changed one detail. When a component suspends, React now commits the nearest fallback **immediately**, and only then pre-renders the suspended siblings in the background. Earlier versions rendered the siblings first, which delayed the fallback. ## How transitions work Wrapping an update in a transition puts it in a **transition lane**: ```tsx const [isPending, startTransition] = useTransition(); function selectTab(next: Tab) { startTransition(() => setTab(next)); } ``` Three behaviours follow: 1. **Interruptible.** If the user clicks or types while the transition renders, React pauses it, handles the urgent update, then restarts the transition from the new state. 2. **No unwanted fallbacks.** If the transition makes **already-visible** content suspend (the new tab's data is loading), React keeps showing the **old** UI and sets `isPending` to `true`, instead of replacing the screen with a spinner. Newly mounted boundaries can still show their fallbacks. This is why routers wrap navigations in transitions: the old page stays interactive until the new one is ready. 3. **Pending state for free.** `isPending` lets you dim the old content or show an inline indicator. In React 19, transitions accept **async functions**, and these are called **Actions**: ```tsx startTransition(async () => { const result = await saveDraft(draft); // State updates after an await are not yet automatically part of the // transition; wrap them again (a documented limitation). startTransition(() => setStatus(result.ok ? "saved" : "error")); }); ``` `isPending` stays `true` for the whole async function. Errors thrown inside an Action propagate to the nearest error boundary. What cannot be a transition: updates that control a text input's value. An input must update synchronously or typing feels broken. The pattern is to split the state: the input value is urgent, and the expensive consequence goes in the transition. ## How useDeferredValue works ```tsx import { useDeferredValue, memo, useState } from "react"; const Results = memo(function Results({ query }: { query: string }) { // expensive: filters and renders thousands of rows return ; }); export function SearchPage() { const [query, setQuery] = useState(""); const deferredQuery = useDeferredValue(query); const stale = query !== deferredQuery; return ( <> setQuery(e.target.value)} />
); } ``` On each keystroke React first renders with the **old** `deferredQuery`, so `Results` is skipped because `memo` sees the same prop. That render commits quickly and the input stays responsive. React then renders again in the background with the new value. Another keystroke abandons that background render. The `memo` is essential: without it, `Results` re-renders on the urgent pass too, and the deferral gains nothing. If the deferred value causes a suspend (the results come from a Suspense data source), the user keeps seeing the old results instead of a fallback. React 19 also added an optional `initialValue` argument (`useDeferredValue(value, initialValue)`) for the first render. **useTransition or useDeferredValue?** | You control... | Use | | --- | --- | | the code that sets the state | `useTransition`: wrap the setter | | only the value (it arrives as a prop, or comes from a hook you do not own) | `useDeferredValue` | | you need an `isPending` flag | `useTransition` (or compare value with deferred value) | **Versus debounce and throttle:** debouncing waits a fixed delay, even on a fast machine where the render would take 5 ms. A deferred render starts immediately, adapts to the device, and is interruptible. But a deferred value does **not** reduce the number of network requests. If each keystroke triggers a fetch, you still want debouncing or request cancellation for the network side. ## Concurrent rendering requirements - **Purity.** Interrupted renders are thrown away and restarted, so render must have no side effects. - **Tearing.** If a component reads a mutable external store (a global variable, a Redux store before v8) during an interruptible render, two components can see different values within one render. `useSyncExternalStore` prevents this: React detects the change and re-renders synchronously. - **Opt-in.** You only get concurrent behaviour for updates you mark as transitions or deferred values, and for Suspense. Everything else behaves as it did before. ## Trade-offs and when not to use them - A transition does not reduce CPU work. A 300 ms render is still 300 ms on a low-end phone. Virtualise or memoise first. - Keeping the old UI visible can confuse users if there is no pending indicator. Always show **something**, such as dimming or a spinner in the tab. - Suspense for data needs a cache, so the resolved promise is reused on retry. Rolling your own is subtle. Use a framework or library. ## Common mistakes and debugging - Wrapping the controlled input's own `setState` in `startTransition`, which makes typing lag or skip characters. - `useDeferredValue` without `memo` on the slow child, which gives no benefit. - Creating the promise inside the component that calls `use()`, which loops forever or refetches on every render. - One giant Suspense boundary at the root, so the whole page blanks on any lazy chunk. - Expecting `useEffect` fetching to show Suspense fallbacks. - **Debugging:** the React DevTools Profiler shows the priority of each commit, and the Chrome Performance panel's React tracks (React 19.2) show the Scheduler lanes (Blocking, Transition, Suspense) on a timeline. ## In the interview **What they probe:** whether you understand that these are scheduling tools rather than performance hacks, why transitions avoid fallbacks, the difference between the two hooks, and how this compares with debouncing. **60-second answer outline:** 1. Suspense shows a fallback when a child suspends on a promise (`use`, `lazy`, framework data). Boundaries are design decisions about reveal order. 2. A transition marks an update as non-urgent: it is interruptible, keeps the old UI instead of re-showing fallbacks, and exposes `isPending`. 3. `useDeferredValue` lags a value so expensive children render in the background. Pair it with `memo`. 4. Neither reduces work, and neither replaces debouncing network calls. 5. All of it depends on pure renders and tear-free stores (`useSyncExternalStore`). **Follow-ups to expect:** Why can't the input's own state be a transition? What changed about sibling rendering when a component suspends in React 19? How does a router use transitions for navigation? What is tearing?
keyPoints: A component suspends on a pending promise via use(), React.lazy or a Suspense-enabled data source, not on useEffect fetching
Transitions are interruptible and keep already-visible UI instead of showing fallbacks, exposing isPending
useDeferredValue lags a value so a memoised slow child renders in the background
Neither reduces CPU work nor replaces debouncing network requests
Concurrent rendering needs pure renders and tear-free external stores (useSyncExternalStore)
interview: How does Suspense know that a component is waiting for data?
useTransition vs useDeferredValue: when do you use each?
Why use a transition instead of debouncing a search input?

check.q: A tab switch is wrapped in startTransition and the new tab's data suspends. What does the user see?
options: The nearest Suspense fallback replaces the current tab immediately
A blank screen until the data arrives
An error boundary
The previous tab stays visible while isPending is true
check.why: Transitions avoid hiding already-revealed content. React keeps the old UI and reports isPending until the new tree is ready.

check.q: You add useDeferredValue for a search query, but typing is still slow. What is the most likely missing piece?
options: The slow results component is not wrapped in memo, so it re-renders on the urgent pass too
useDeferredValue only works inside Server Components
You must also call flushSync
The input must be uncontrolled
check.why: The urgent render passes the old deferred value. Without memo the expensive child re-renders anyway, so nothing is deferred.

check.q: Why should you not wrap a controlled text input's own setState in startTransition?
options: Transitions cannot update strings
It causes a hydration mismatch
Input value updates must be synchronous; a deferrable update makes typing lag or drop characters
startTransition only works in event handlers on buttons
check.why: Split the state: the input value stays urgent, and the expensive consequence of it goes in the transition.

lessons.title: Component API patterns: compound, controlled, headless
lessons.summary: Compound components, controlled vs uncontrolled APIs, render props vs hooks, headless components and composition over configuration, with the trade-offs interviewers probe.
keyPoints: Prefer composition and children over growing configuration props; it is inversion of control
Compound components share implicit state through context so callers arrange the parts freely
Support controlled and uncontrolled modes with a controllable-state hook decided at mount
Hooks replaced most render props; render props remain when the component must place caller-rendered UI
Headless primitives own behaviour and accessibility; the design system owns the styling
interview: How would you build a compound component like Tabs?
Render props vs custom hooks: when is each still the right tool?
What is a headless component and why do design systems build on them?

check.q: Why is context preferred over React.Children.map with cloneElement for compound components?
options: cloneElement is removed in React 19
Context keeps working when callers wrap or conditionally render the parts; cloning only reaches direct children
Context never causes re-renders
cloneElement cannot pass props
check.why: Cloning inspects direct children only, so wrapping a trigger in a div breaks it. Context reaches any depth.

check.q: React warns that a component is changing an uncontrolled input to be controlled. What is the usual cause?
options: Using defaultValue and onChange together
Rendering the input inside a form
Using a key on the input
The value prop started as undefined and later became a string
check.why: value={undefined} means uncontrolled. When it becomes a string the input switches mode. Initialise with an empty string.

check.q: Which is the best fit for a render prop rather than a hook?
options: Sharing debounce logic between components
Reading the current theme
A virtualised list that decides which rows exist while the caller decides how each row looks
Fetching the current user
check.why: The list owns placement and lifecycle of rows; the caller supplies how each renders. That is the case render props still serve best.

lessons.title: React 19: Actions, useOptimistic, use() and the Compiler
lessons.summary: Actions and form handling, useActionState, useFormStatus, useOptimistic, the use() API, ref as a prop, metadata hoisting, React 19.2 additions and what the React Compiler changes.
keyPoints: Actions are async functions run in transitions with built-in pending state, error propagation and form reset
useActionState returns state, a wrapped action and isPending; calls are queued in order
useFormStatus reads the parent form only; useOptimistic overlays state that reverts when the action settles
use() reads promises and context, can be called conditionally, and suspends on pending promises
The React Compiler auto-memoises code that follows the Rules of React, making manual useMemo the exception
interview: How does useOptimistic work, and what happens when the action fails?
What does the use() API do, and why can it be called conditionally?
What changed about refs in React 19?

check.q: A SubmitButton calls useFormStatus but is rendered in the same component that renders the form element. What does pending report?
options: Always false, because useFormStatus only reads a form rendered above the calling component
Always true
The correct pending state
It throws an error
check.why: useFormStatus behaves like reading context from a parent form. Move the button into its own component rendered inside the form.

check.q: An Action calls addOptimistic(newItem) and then the server call throws. What happens to the optimistic item?
options: It stays until the page reloads
It is saved locally and retried
React keeps it and logs a warning
It disappears when the action settles, because the UI falls back to the real state
check.why: Optimistic state only lives while the action is pending. Informing the user about the failure is still your job.

check.q: With the React Compiler enabled, which use of useMemo is still worth keeping?
options: Memoising a cheap string concatenation
Memoising every inline callback passed to a DOM element
Keeping a stable object identity that an effect depends on for correctness
None; the compiler errors on manual useMemo
check.why: The compiler handles performance memoisation. Keep manual memoisation where referential identity matters for correctness.
